newsitem.title: INDIA: FT sees more overseas than UK sales in 2-3 yrs.
newsitem.headline: FT sees more overseas than UK sales in 2-3 yrs.

text.p: The Financial Times, Britain's heavyweight business newspaper, will have a larger circulation overseas than domestically within two to three years, Andrew Gilchrist, managing director of Financial Times International told Reuters.

The pink business daily, owned by Pearson Plc publishing group, will raise its circulation to 400,000 from a current 300,000 in the next five years, doubling its growth rate, Gilchrist said in an interview.

That surge will be achieved by doubling circulation in both the United States and Asia-Pacific, while consolidating the newspaper's pre-eminent position as Europe's favourite business daily, the 38-year-old former army officer said.
"In about two, maybe three, years' time we will have a larger circulation outside the U.K. than inside the U.K., which I think is quite an important milestone for us to achieve," he said.

Gilchrist is in India to meet leading businessmen and bankers, along with government officials, and is drumming up support for a survey in June of the country which will coincide with 50 years of independence from British rule.
Gilchrist, who in 1994 was appointed director for electronic publishing for the FT, including on the Internet, said the FT had been surprised by the growth of that market.
The FT was looking forward to earn more revenues from its growing international subscriber base through the on-line edition of the newspaper, he said.
"We have grown from nothing to over a quarter million in three-quarters of the year in terms of registrations, so we really have been quite taken aback by the growth of that."
"We have also curiously found it an extremely efficient way for growing our international subscriptions," he said.
"They have become so important as a form of subscriptions that they are actually budgeted this year," Gilchrist said.
"We knew we could get quite a few from the Internet, so that's good news."

The Financial Times has made inroads into a number of countries through tie-ups with domestic newspapers, chosen for their editorial quality, but it ran into a roadblock when it tried to go down this track into India.

The Indian government last August stalled the Financial Times' attempt to take a stake in the Calcutta-based Business Standard newspaper, citing a 40-year-old cabinet decision barring foreign media from publishing in India.
Gilchrist said that had effectively killed the deal, although interest could be revived if the regulations changed. But other options for entry into India would be considered too.

"But there are no specific or different plans and fundamentally the situation hasn't changed. Government regulations haven't changed," he said, noting that the FT had overcome similar obstacles elsewhere.

"In Canada there are also government restrictions on foreign media (but in South Africa) we own 25 percent of the Financial Post, we've just bought 50 percent of Business Day." "We have met largely success, in fact more often than not because people approach us." Gilchrist said the FT had considered the strategy taken by its American rival the Wall Street Journal, which prints a page packaged for the local readership in a domestic newspaper, the Indian Express.
"It is something that we have looked at in the past," he said, citing the four to eight page insert Financial Izvestia in the Russian daily Izvestia as the most successful example.
"In other places it has been more interesting for us to form a proper relationship with a major business newspaper as in France or Spain," Gilchrist said.
